strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck in ultra-high-resolution optical flow: RAFT-style all-pairs correlation volume sampling has quadratic memory/computation, while on-demand sampling is slow and hardware-unfriendly. The proposed block-sparse exact sampling operator is a relevant and useful systems/algorithmic contribution.

The method is motivated by a clear empirical analysis: only a small regular fraction of the 4D correlation volume is actually sampled (about 1.6% on average), and patch-major/block-aware layout further increases sparsity. This analysis directly informs the algorithm design.

Technical design is sound: computation mask generation, block sparse matrix multiplication, patch-major input layout, and incremental caching across recurrent iterations. The paper reports near-zero (0.03%) endpoint error difference versus the official RAFT implementation, supporting the claim that the operator is mathematically equivalent.

Extensive isolated benchmarking across input resolutions, GPU models (RTX 3090/4090, A100, GH200), feature dimensionality, and iteration counts. The method achieves up to 90% faster runtime than on-demand sampling and up to 95% lower memory than the dense default implementation, with sub-quadratic O(n^1.5) space complexity.

End-to-end evaluation includes a newly generated 8K ultra-high-resolution dataset from Blender's Charge, plus Sintel, KITTI, and Spring benchmarks. The cascaded inference extension improves large-motion estimation on 8K and enables RAFT-based methods to run at resolutions where the default implementation fails out-of-memory.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameters, unit tests, and the Blender scene setup script are provided. The paper also reports hardware and library versions.
The work has clear potential usefulness for movie post-production and other UHR video tasks, where high-quality flow at native resolution is needed but dense correlation volumes are prohibitive.
weaknesses: The core contribution is primarily an efficient implementation of an existing mathematical operator rather than a new optical flow architecture or learning method. While valuable, it may be viewed as engineering optimization rather than a fundamental methodological advance.

The UHR accuracy evaluation relies on a synthetic dataset generated from only three Blender Charge sequences (335 frames). This limited diversity may not fully capture real-world UHR flow challenges, and the dataset is not clearly stated to be publicly released.

Isolated correlation-sampling experiments compare only the default RAFT, on-demand sampling, and the proposed method. Other efficient correlation or high-resolution flow approaches are not included in the isolated analysis, and end-to-end comparisons are constrained by out-of-memory failures for many baselines.

Several hyperparameters, such as block size B, cache growth factor, and the 5GB cache overhead limit, appear empirically chosen. Sensitivity to these choices and failure modes under extreme motion are not deeply analyzed.

The abstract/end-to-end savings claims are resolution- and hardware-dependent. At low resolution, Table 3 shows the proposed method can be slower than the default RAFT implementation, so the benefits are mainly at high resolutions rather than universal.

The cascaded inference extension is a simple multi-resolution warm-start heuristic. Its gains are demonstrated empirically, but the paper does not deeply analyze why it interacts well with the efficient sampling algorithm or whether it introduces additional approximation beyond the exact sampling operator.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim on 8K is somewhat qualified: SEA-RAFT (Cascaded) achieves best 1px and large-motion metrics, but its EPE is not the best among all methods at feasible scales (e.g., MS-RAFT+ at 4096 has lower EPE). The claim should be interpreted carefully.

At the largest resolution (8192), memory usage of the proposed method is similar to on-demand sampling (e.g., RAFT 19.42GB vs 19.40GB), so the memory advantage over the feasible on-demand baseline is not substantial there; the main advantage is runtime.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: ultra-high-resolution (UHR) optical flow estimation, where existing RAFT-based methods either run out of memory or fail to capture large motion at native resolution.

Well-supported empirical motivation: the authors instrument RAFT on Sintel and show that only ~1.6% of correlation-volume cells are actually sampled on average, providing concrete justification for a block-sparse formulation. The patch-major layout observation (Fig. 3) is a useful, non-obvious insight that substantially increases block-level sparsity without computational overhead.

The proposed sampler exactly matches RAFT's mathematical operator (reported 0.03% EPE difference), making it a genuine drop-in replacement that requires no retraining. This is a valuable property for the community and is validated with unit tests.

Comprehensive and systematic evaluation: isolated correlation-sampling benchmarks across input resolution, iteration count, feature dimensionality, and multiple GPUs (RTX 3090/4090, A100, GH200); component-level runtime breakdown (Table 1); caching ablation; and end-to-end results on the new 8K dataset plus Sintel/KITTI/Spring.

A new 8K optical flow benchmark derived from Blender Charge (335 frames at 8192x3432 with 16K-rendered ground truth) is a tangible contribution that fills a gap in UHR flow evaluation, and the dataset generation script and sequence details are provided for reproducibility.

The cascaded test-time inference extension reduces large-motion endpoint error (magnitude >128px) substantially (~80% on the 8K data) without additional training, and the paper is transparent about its relation to RAFT's warm-start and MS-RAFT+.
Good reproducibility: pseudocode (Algorithm 1), sub-quadratic O(n^1.5) memory-complexity derivation, hardware/software configuration, and block-size settings are all documented.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea (computing only the block-sparse subset of the correlation volume that will be sampled, with incremental caching across iterations) is relatively straightforward once the access-pattern observation is made. The novelty is more engineering than conceptual, and the cascaded inference is essentially a multi-resolution warm-start initialization similar in spirit to prior warm-start/MS-RAFT ideas.

The new dataset is limited to a single Blender movie (Charge), only three sequences and 335 frames, and is entirely synthetic. This limits diversity and raises questions about generalization and the domain gap to real UHR footage (e.g., film, sports, satellite), which weakens the generality of the 'state-of-the-art at 8K' claim.

The reported benefits are strongly concentrated at very high resolutions. At low resolutions the method is on par with the default (Fig. 5, Table 1) and carries notable overhead from mask construction and cache updates; the paper itself notes the gains come mainly at high resolutions.

Memory comparison is nuanced and somewhat ambiguously framed. Table 3 shows that at high resolution the proposed method can use more memory than on-demand sampling (e.g., 17.21 GiB vs 10.25 GiB at 8192 in one row), so the memory advantage is relative to the dense Default implementation, not to on-demand; the abstract's phrasing ('similar memory savings compared to the default') would benefit from clearer scoping.

End-to-end runtime improvements apply only to methods that use correlation-volume sampling (the RAFT family). Competitive approaches such as FlowFormer/FlowFormer++ and GMFlow do not benefit, which limits the breadth of the practical impact.

The block size B is chosen heuristically (8, or 16 for MS-RAFT+/CCMR at high resolution) and is not adaptively selected; the sensitivity analysis is partial, and the trade-off between block size and cache/memory overhead is not fully characterized.

On established benchmarks (Sintel, KITTI, Spring; Tables 8-10) the improvements are modest and occasionally 0%, so the strongest quantitative evidence rests largely on the newly introduced synthetic 8K dataset.

strengths: Targets a real and important bottleneck: the quadratic cost and memory of dense all-pairs correlation volumes, which is precisely what limits RAFT-style methods on ultra-high-resolution inputs.

The proposed block-sparse correlation sampler is mathematically consistent with the RAFT operator (verified to ~0.03% endpoint error), so it is a drop-in, accuracy-preserving efficiency improvement rather than a lossy approximation.

Empirical efficiency claims are well supported: measured speedups over on-demand sampling (up to ~90%) and memory reductions over the dense default (up to ~95%), with thorough sweeps over resolution, feature dimensionality, iteration count, and four GPUs (RTX 3090/4090, A100, GH200).

Adds a new 8K rendered benchmark (Blender Charge) with ground-truth flow and a training-free cascaded inference extension that substantially improves large-motion estimation, plus a detailed component breakdown and complexity analysis.

Presentation is clear and well organized, with informative figures (access-pattern visualizations, algorithm overview), pseudocode, an O(n^1.5) complexity derivation, and a scene-setup script for dataset generation.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The core contribution is essentially a block-sparse matrix multiplication with a precomputed mask and cross-iteration caching applied to an already-intuitive observation (local lookups touch few cells); the 'analysis' mostly confirms what is expected rather than revealing new insight.

The method carries substantial non-compute overhead. Table 1 shows mask setting (~20%) and cache updating (~36%) dominating at 1024px, and the paper itself concedes the approach only wins at high resolutions while being 'on par' with the dense default at low resolution; the practical benefit is thus confined to extreme resolutions where the dense default already OOMs.

The headline accuracy gains come from the separate, simple cascaded test-time inference, not from the correlation sampler, and the 'state-of-the-art' claim is selective: EPE at feasible scales (e.g., 2.70) is worse than MS-RAFT+ (1.92/1.63), and the cascaded extension is validated only on SEA-RAFT.

The memory claim is overstated in framing: peak memory is comparable to or worse than the on-demand sampler (e.g., SEA-RAFT at 8192px: 17.2 vs 10.25 GiB), so the '95% lower memory' is only relative to the dense default, not to the most memory-efficient baseline.

Effective sparsity is far lower than the headline 1.6% figure once realistic block sizes are used (roughly 8-28% in Table 4), which weakens the motivating premise and reduces the theoretical headroom.

Accuracy evaluation for the 8K setting rests entirely on a small, synthetic, rendered dataset (3 sequences, 335 frames); there is no real-world UHR evaluation, limiting the generality of the accuracy conclusions.
